companies.description: Designs GPUs and AI chips that power most large-scale AI training and data centers.
companies.story: Nvidia grew revenue by 17.9% this quarter, extending its streak to 11 straight quarters of growth, while net income and EPS each edged up modestly (around 2-3%). Cash on hand jumped nearly 70%, giving the company a much larger cushion, though this coincided with debt nearly quadrupling (up 293.9%) — a sharp shift worth watching to understand what the borrowed money is funding. Gross margin held essentially flat at 75%, showing that profitability per dollar of sales stayed steady even as the top line surged.

company_story.label: What it does
company_story.answer: NVIDIA designs GPUs and AI accelerator chips (plus the CUDA software stack and networking gear) and sells them to companies that build and run AI systems, essentially selling the "picks and shovels" of the AI computing buildout rather than running AI applications itself.

company_story.label: Who its customers are
company_story.answer: Its customers are cloud providers (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Oracle), AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic), large enterprises building AI infrastructure, and to a lesser extent gaming PC makers and automotive/robotics companies.

company_story.label: Competitive edge
company_story.answer: The moat is the combination of raw chip performance, the CUDA software ecosystem that developers have built on for over a decade, and full-stack integration (chips, networking, systems, software) that makes switching to competitors costly and technically risky.

company_story.label: Leadership
company_story.answer: Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO since 1993, still leads the company — this is from general knowledge and could be out of date if there's been a very recent change.

company_story.label: Insider ownership
company_story.answer: Requires manual research — there's no free, keyless, reliable source for insider ownership percentage. Check the company's most recent DEF 14A proxy statement on SEC EDGAR (the "Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners and Management" table) for the real number.

company_story.label: Growth potential
company_story.answer: Growth potential is tied to continued buildout of AI data center infrastructure, expansion into new markets like robotics, autonomous vehicles, and enterprise AI software, and international demand, though the pace of the last few years' growth is unlikely to be sustained indefinitely.

company_story.label: Risks
company_story.answer: Key risks include customer concentration (a handful of hyperscalers drive a large share of revenue), competition from custom chips built by those same customers (Google TPUs, Amazon Trainium), export restrictions on China sales, potential AI capital spending slowdown, and the recent sharp increase in debt whose purpose isn't yet clear.

company_story.label: What you're paying
company_story.answer: The business trades at a trailing P/E of 26.5; EV/EBITDA is not available due to missing or negative EBITDA data.

company_story.label: Market cap today
company_story.answer: $5.11T, from Nasdaq's public quote data — the market's price on the whole business, not a per-share number.

company_story.label: The 5-10 year case
company_story.answer: A materially higher market cap in five to ten years would require AI infrastructure spending to keep growing for years, NVIDIA to maintain its technological lead over custom silicon and rival GPU makers, and margins to hold up despite customers' efforts to reduce dependence on it; a stagnant or lower valuation could result if any of those falter or if AI capex growth simply matures like past computing cycles.

company_story.label: Risk / reward
company_story.answer: If the AI buildout continues and NVIDIA holds its position, the business could be worth substantially more than today given how early large-scale AI infrastructure spending may still be; if growth slows sharply, customers succeed in shifting to in-house chips, or the current spending proves to be overbuilt capacity, the business's earnings power and valuation could contract significantly, and at a $5.11T starting size even modest percentage disappointments represent enormous dollar amounts.

companies.description: Makes the iPhone, Mac, and services like the App Store and iCloud.
companies.story: Apple's profits and earnings per share ticked up slightly even as revenue slipped 1.6%, thanks to improved efficiency: gross margin rose to 50.1%, extending a four-quarter streak of margin gains, and debt edged lower. Cash on hand dropped a notable 13.2%, though nothing in the numbers here explains why. The bigger caution sign is that operating expenses grew 0.9% while revenue shrank—the second straight quarter costs have outpaced sales—meaning the company is spending more to earn less, a pattern that could squeeze profits down the road if it continues.

company_story.label: What it does
company_story.answer: Apple designs and sells premium hardware — iPhone, Mac, iPad, Watch — and layers a growing services business (App Store, iCloud, Apple Music, AppleCare, advertising, payments) on top, monetizing a large installed base of devices over time.

company_story.label: Who its customers are
company_story.answer: Its customers are consumers and businesses globally who want tightly integrated, premium hardware and software, skewing toward higher-income buyers in the U.S., Europe, and China, plus a large recurring base of existing iPhone/Mac/iPad owners who buy services and upgrades.

company_story.label: Competitive edge
company_story.answer: The moat comes from ecosystem lock-in (iMessage, iCloud, Apple Watch pairing, AirDrop), a tightly controlled hardware-software-services integration that's hard to replicate, brand loyalty, and high switching costs once someone owns multiple Apple devices tied together.

company_story.label: Leadership
company_story.answer: Tim Cook is CEO, a role he's held since 2011 after succeeding Steve Jobs; this is based on general knowledge and could be outdated if there's been a very recent leadership change.

company_story.label: Insider ownership
company_story.answer: Requires manual research — there's no free, keyless, reliable source for insider ownership percentage. Check the company's most recent DEF 14A proxy statement on SEC EDGAR (the "Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners and Management" table) for the real number.

company_story.label: Growth potential
company_story.answer: Growth is currently stalled at the top line (0 straight quarters of revenue growth) even as gross margins have expanded for 4 straight quarters, so future growth potential rests on services expansion, new product categories (like wearables or future AI-driven features), and eventual hardware upgrade cycles rather than current momentum.

company_story.label: Risks
company_story.answer: Key risks include revenue growth having stopped, operating expenses growing faster than revenue for two straight quarters, heavy reliance on iPhone sales, regulatory pressure on App Store fees globally, and geopolitical/supply chain exposure concentrated in China.

company_story.label: What you're paying
company_story.answer: The stock trades at a trailing P/E of 37.5; EV/EBITDA is not available due to missing or negative EBITDA data, so that comparison can't be made.

company_story.label: Market cap today
company_story.answer: $4.84T, from Nasdaq's public quote data — the market's price on the whole business, not a per-share number.

company_story.label: The 5-10 year case
company_story.answer: For the market cap to grow meaningfully from $4.84T, revenue growth would need to resume and the current opex-outgrowing-revenue trend would need to reverse, likely requiring a new services or product growth driver (such as AI-integrated features or new device categories) to reaccelerate the top line while sustaining margins.

company_story.label: Risk / reward
company_story.answer: Without a share price or explicit future multiple/growth assumption to model, no numeric return can be responsibly estimated here; qualitatively, the risk/reward hinges on whether growth resumes and margins hold — if operating costs keep outpacing flat-to-declining revenue, profitability could erode even as the business remains large and profitable in absolute terms.

companies.story: Micron had a strong quarter: revenue climbed 30.8% and net income rose 33.5%, while profitability also improved as gross margin expanded from 84.6% to 86.8%. The company's financial position got healthier too, with cash on hand up 53.4% and debt cut by 68.4%. This marks the sixth straight quarter of both revenue growth and margin expansion, suggesting the memory and storage chip business has been on a sustained upswing rather than a one-time bounce.

company_story.label: What it does
company_story.answer: Micron designs and manufactures memory and storage chips — DRAM (short-term memory) and NAND flash (storage) — that are essential, interchangeable components built into computers, phones, servers, and other electronics, and sells them as commodity-like semiconductors at massive scale.

company_story.label: Who its customers are
company_story.answer: Its customers are PC makers, smartphone manufacturers, data center and cloud operators, automakers, and industrial electronics companies — essentially any business that builds devices needing memory or storage.

company_story.label: Competitive edge
company_story.answer: Micron competes on manufacturing scale, process technology, and cost efficiency in a market with only three major DRAM players (Micron, Samsung, SK Hynix) and a handful of NAND makers; its edge is being one of a small number of companies capable of producing memory at the leading edge and at volume, not a sticky brand or switching-cost moat.

company_story.label: Leadership
company_story.answer: Sanjay Mehrotra is CEO, a role he has held since 2017; this is from general knowledge and may be out of date if there's been a very recent change.

company_story.label: Insider ownership
company_story.answer: Requires manual research — there's no free, keyless, reliable source for insider ownership percentage. Check the company's most recent DEF 14A proxy statement on SEC EDGAR (the "Security Ownership of Certain Beneficial Owners and Management" table) for the real number.

company_story.label: Growth potential
company_story.answer: Growth is tied to rising memory content per device (AI servers, smartphones, cars) and cyclical price recoveries; the current streak of 6 straight quarters of revenue growth and margin expansion reflects a strong upswing driven in part by AI-related demand for high-bandwidth memory.

company_story.label: Risks
company_story.answer: Memory is a brutally cyclical, commodity business where prices can swing wildly based on industry-wide supply and demand, capital spending is enormous, and a downturn in PC/phone/server demand or oversupply from competitors can quickly erase margins and profits.

company_story.label: What you're paying
company_story.answer: On the given numbers — trailing P/E of 11.7 and trailing EV/EBITDA of 8.8 — the market is pricing Micron cheaply relative to typical growth-stock multiples, consistent with investors treating it as a cyclical business currently near a profit peak rather than a steadily compounding grower.

company_story.label: Market cap today
company_story.answer: $994.3B, from Nasdaq's public quote data — the market's price on the whole business, not a per-share number.

company_story.label: The 5-10 year case
company_story.answer: A meaningfully larger market cap in five to ten years would require sustained structural demand growth (AI, data centers) to smooth out the historical boom-bust cycle, continued discipline among the three major DRAM producers to avoid oversupply, and Micron maintaining technological parity with Samsung and SK Hynix; without those, the market cap could just as easily cycle back down as memory prices revert.

company_story.label: Risk / reward
company_story.answer: Because Micron is priced at a low multiple during a strong part of its cycle, an investor could gain significantly if AI-driven demand extends the upcycle and multiples re-rate upward, but could lose substantially if memory prices collapse in the next downturn, since both earnings and the multiple investors are willing to pay tend to fall together in this industry.
